title: The meeting
hookLine: you will see your Lord as you see this moon, without crowding
tomorrow: what's the first word said at the door of home?

cards: A full moon over a parking lot stops people mid-step. Phones come out, and everyone looks at the same thing at once, with nobody blocking anybody's view.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ used that very sight to answer yesterday's question. In Sahih al-Bukhari, his companions are sitting with him on a night of the full moon.
He looks up and says: you will see your Lord as you see this moon, without crowding to see Him.

teach.b: The Qur'an says it too, in Pickthall's words: "That day will faces be resplendent, Looking toward their Lord." In Arabic the two words almost rhyme: nadirah, radiant, and nazirah, looking.
Faces lit by what they're looking at.
A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when the veil is lifted, nothing the people of the Garden were given will be dearer to them than looking at their Lord.
Here's the honest part: Muslims have argued about what this seeing means. Sunni theologians affirm a real seeing, without asking how.
The Mu'tazila, an early school of thought, read it as a figure of speech for awaiting His reward. And the Qur'an also says that no vision grasps Him.
The Sunni answer holds both: seen, never fully grasped. That is the meeting this whole stretch has been getting ready for. Not a courtroom only.
A face turned toward a face.
A friend might like this one: the Prophet's picture for seeing God was a clear moon, the kind of sight nobody has to push to see.

how: Sunni Muslims affirm that the believers will see Allah in the Garden, without saying how, citing Qur'an 75:22–23 and the moon hadith; some recite these verses and ask in their prayers for the joy of looking at Allah's face.

o: standing before Allah to have your deeds weighed
reuniting with your family members after death
the believers seeing their Lord in the Garden

games.q: what's inside the teaching — tap the pairs.
p: read it as awaiting His reward

s: in the hadith, people will have to push and crowd to see
as you see this moon: without crowding.
the Qur'an says faces will be resplendent, looking toward their Lord
Muslims have always agreed on what seeing Allah means
Sunni theologians affirm a real seeing without asking how; the Mu'tazila read it as a figure of speech.

games.q: a Muslim friend asks, 'we'll SEE Allah? doesn't that mean He has a body?' which answer stays closest to what the tradition teaches?
o: Sunni teaching: a real seeing, without asking how; no vision grasps Him.
it only means seeing His reward; every school agrees on that.
yes; the Qur'an describes in detail what He looks like.
games.why: Sunni theologians hold both verses together: faces looking toward their Lord (75:23) and no vision grasps Him (6:103). seen, never fully grasped.

practice: If you can see the sky, find the moon; if not, any light will do: a lamp, a window, a candle. Look at it softly for a few breaths without picking up your phone, and notice how the light reaches you without your reaching for it.
Let a little longing sit there with you.

wordCard.voice: The meeting: the believers' seeing of their Lord in the Garden, which the Qur'an and the hadith describe and the Prophet compared to a clear moon.

orig.note: Arabic: the seeing of Allah, the theologians' name for this teaching.

carryVoice: Hold two words tonight: faces radiant, lit by what they're looking at. Goodnight under whatever moon you've got.

sources.q: That day will faces be resplendent, Looking toward their Lord.
